episodes.170437: Precipitable water values in excess of 150% of normal occurred across western Colorado as monsoon moisture continued to stream into the region. As a result, widespread showers and thunderstorms developed. Weak steering flow aloft resulted in slow moving storms. Additionally, storms produced heavy rain. Flash flooding and a debris flow occurred in Ouray County as a result of the heavy rain. Another localized debris flow occurred in Rio Blanco County.
episodes.170439: A weak surface low and boundary moved across a marginally unstable air mass across Ontario and New York during the afternoon of July 28th. Several thunderstorms developed across Ontario and then moved into New York and continued to develop. Many of these storms contained heavy rain and lightning with one isolated storm that produced marginal wind damage to trees.
episodes.170440: Abundant monsoon moisture remained over the Four Corners region. This led to another round of showers and thunderstorms across southwest Colorado. Storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain. As a result of the heavy rain, a debris flow occurred in Ouray County on Imogene Pass with some other mudslides reported in Archuleta County. Additionally, gusty outflow winds in excess of 60 mph occurred across portions of Rio Blanco County.
episodes.170447: A weak surface low and boundary moved across a marginally unstable air mass across New York and Vermont during the afternoon and early evening of July 28th. Several thunderstorms developed across New York and moved into Vermont and continued to develop. Many of these storms contained heavy rain and lightning with two isolated storms that produced marginal wind damage to trees.
episodes.170647: A cold front approaching southern New England triggered one isolated severe thunderstorm in western Massachusetts during the evening.
episodes.170744: Isolated minor wind damage accompanied several severe storms. A weak frontal boundary was draped from the Great Lakes region to the Ozarks of Missouri. A small complex of thunderstorms formed along this boundary during the heat of the late afternoon and early evening hours. Surface dew points in the mid to upper 70's contributed to a very unstable atmosphere. Mixed layer capes were over 3000 j/kg.
episodes.170835: A couple isolated thunderstorms produced minor wind damage.
episodes.170872: A few thunderstorms produced localized gusty winds over the area waterways.
episodes.170947: A line of storms developed ahead of a cold front as it swept across Central New York. Damaging winds from a few storms knocked down trees and wires across the region. A couple of the downed trees landed on structures, resulting in some damage.
episodes.170990: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind and hail, along with torrential rainfall across the I-25 Corridor and Northeast Plains.  Areas hardest hit included:  eastern Boulder, Douglas, eastern Larimer, Washington and Weld counties.  Hail up to tennis ball size (2.5 inches), was observed near Black Hollow Reservoir east of Fort Collins.  Elsewhere the hail ranged from quarter to golfball size.  The hail damaged homes and vehicles.  Strong winds also produced some tree damage.  Torrential rainfall produced extensive street flooding around Fort Collins.  Torrential rain and small hail also occurred in the town of Estes Park. The hail piled up to a foot deep in spots, and had to be removed using snowplows. People in the community helped drivers dig out cars and clear the roadway on East Elkhorn Avenue.  Minor flooding also occurred in some of the nearby businesses.  Minor flash flooding was also observed in Washington County.
episodes.170991: A few severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds and hail.  In Larimer County, the wind knocked down three trees and snapped branches.  In Washington County, hail up to quarter size was reported.
episodes.171110: A cluster of thunderstorms produced some isolated wind damage in southeastern Pennsylvania.
episodes.171176: A large complex of thunderstorms moved east across southern Illinois during the afternoon and evening hours. Very heavy rainfall rates contributed to isolated instances of flash flooding. The complex of thunderstorms developed ahead of a 500 mb disturbance over central Missouri, which moved eastward into a very moist and unstable air mass. Precipitable water values were around 2.25 inches, and surface-based cape exceeded 2000 J/kg. Soils across the region were quite moist due to repeated thunderstorms in the preceding several days.
episodes.171189: A frontal boundary remained parked over the Central Appalachians on the last week of July, which kept southwest Virginia suseptible to heavy downpours from daily showers and thunderstorms for a prolonged period of time. Copious amounts of late evening rain on the 27th resulted in nighttime flash flooding in Dickenson County, where pockets of 2 to 4 inches fell. Local creeks and streams rose out of their banks early in the morning of July 28th and resulted in water on roadways and washing out several residential bridges north of Clintwood. High water also entered into the Clintwood Public Library overnight and flooded the first floor of the building.
episodes.171617: Isolated strong to locally severe storms briefly resulted in hail up to the size of quarters and wind gusts near 60 MPH for some communities.
episodes.171618: A few strong to severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Wyoming during the late afternoon and early evening on July 27th. This activity mainly produced strong wind gusts to 60+ MPH, along with a few reports of quarter to golf ball sized hail.
episodes.171729: Supercells moved through southwest Nebraska during the late evening of July 27, producing severe hail and wind gusts, some significant up to 80 mph.
episodes.171911: An upper level ridge was centered east of the area and another to the west. That put the local area in a region of weakness between them which is an area conducive for higher rain chances. The upper air soundings around that time showed sufficient instability and ample moisture in place to support numerous thunderstorm development. The local precipitable water value was well over 2 inches which provided the potential for heavy rainfall. One storm developed around Baton Rouge in the afternoon. For a short period, new development occurred in the same location while the storm itself moved northward. That non-movement and thus continued heavy rain resulted in flash flooding.
episodes.171956: During the evening scattered strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast into East Central Colorado.  Hail up to grapefruit size was reported near Wauneta.  The storms went on to produce wind gusts up to 71 MPH near Idalia.  Wind gusts from the thunderstorms broke off small tree limbs and tossed a pool cover near Bethune.  Behind the severe storms, a large area of moderate rainfall moved in later in the night.  Some of this rainfall fell on ground which had received a couple inches of rainfall a couple days ago.  The additional three to five inches of rainfall caused flooding to occur in the central part of Kit Carson County which lasted into the following day.
episodes.171961: A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms moved over far Southwest Nebraska from the northwest.  Hail up to dime size was reported near Max and near Stratton.  The strongest wind gust reported of 60 MPH was reported in Benkelman.  As thunderstorms rolled through Trenton, the ethanol plant was struck by lightning at some point, causing unspecified but significant damage which took three days to repair.
episodes.171976: A few thunderstorms became severe in late July on the 28th and 30th along a quasi-stationary boundary draped across northern sections of the state. Severe storms were mainly oriented along a west to east line adjacent to the frontal boundary.
episodes.172108: A high based thunderstorm moving off the higher terrain of southeast Colorado produced one severe wind gust.
episodes.172128: A northward lifting warm front brought a hot and humid air mass to portions of eastern New York on July 28, 2022. Heat indices reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across the Hudson River Valley from the Capital District and points south. ||During the afternoon and early evening hours, showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front. A couple of these storms became severe producing isolated wind damage across portions of Rensselaer and Columbia counties.
episodes.172129: A thunderstorm developed across northwestern Connecticut during the early evening hours on July 28, 2022 producing a weak EF-0 tornado near Colebrook, which downed some trees and damaged some structures along its path.
episodes.172188: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a cold front in central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 28th. Several downbursts occurred producing winds of 60-65 mph and scattered reports of damage.
episodes.172220: A few strong to severe storms developed over southwest and central Missouri on the afternoon of the 27th south of Interstate 44.
episodes.172308: Central NC was largely under the influence of a mid-level ridge of high pressure. There also existed strong westerly flow at mid-levels further to the north across the upper Mississippi Valley into the northern Mid-Atlantic. An Appalachian lee trough was present across western NC, which forced some isolated to scattered showers and storms during the afternoon and evening, persisting as isolated storms into the early overnight hours. There was one severe storm that produced several downed trees and powerlines in Warren County.

episodes.172369: During the mid-to-late afternoon hours on July 27th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed immediately ahead of a quasi-stationary surface frontal boundary located near the Ohio River. Across central Kentucky, temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dewpoints in the mid 70s provided copious amounts of instability, with convection having mixed-layer CAPE in excess of 3000 J/kg to work with. During the mid-afternoon period, showers and thunderstorms developed along the Western Kentucky and Bluegrass Parkways and moved steadily to the south and east. The strongest storms produced isolated wind damage, mainly across south central Kentucky. While most of the severe threat subsided during the overnight hours, persistent convection across south central Kentucky created isolated flash flooding issues.||During the evening hours of July 28th, a secondary weak frontal boundary helped to spark convection across portions of Kentucky, causing isolated wind damage in Meade County.
episodes.172376: A line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Ontario during the morning into midday. This line of thunderstorms produced severe marine thunderstorm winds before moving east of the lake by early afternoon.
episodes.172448: An inverted trough moving westward near the Arizona/New Mexico border aided in thunderstorm development during the afternoon of the 27th across far eastern Arizona. Thunderstorms progressed toward the west before reaching southern Gila County late in the afternoon. Deep monsoonal moisture, with PWATs in excess of 1.70, resulted in thunderstorms being efficient rainfall producers. In the Globe area, rainfall amounts upwards of 1.70 in an hour were reported. Heavy rainfall in the area led to isolated flash flooding near the San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation line along with several reports of minor flooding in the Globe area. No damage or injuries were reported.
episodes.172519: During the early AM hours of 7/28, a squall line produced extensive damage in Minneapolis, KS with winds estimated as high as 95 mph per conclusions from an NWS survey.
episodes.172552: As a result of instability within the atmosphere, scattered thunderstorms broke out over the western and south-central Texas Panhandle during the evening of the 28th. Severe wind gusts were reported across the aforementioned areas of the Texas Panhandle, including some wind damage.
episodes.172563: Between July 25th and July 30th, 2022, several complexes of training thunderstorms developed south of I-64 and brought heavy rain, deadly flash flooding, and devastating river flooding to eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia. These thunderstorms, at times, caused rainfall rates in excess of 4/hr across complex terrain that led to widespread devastating impacts. While it did not rain continuously during this 4-day stretch, the overwhelming amounts of rain and resultant flooding led to 39 deaths and widespread catastrophic damage. Entire homes and parts of some communities were swept away by flood waters, leading to costly damage to infrastructure in the region. Over 600 helicopter rescues and countless swift water rescues by boat were needed to evacuate people who were trapped by the quickly-rising flood waters. In total, 24 Flash Flood Warnings were issued between July 26th and July 30th. Between the evening of July 27th and the mid-morning hours on July 28th (the peak of the event), 13 warnings were issued, 3 of which were upgraded to a Flash Flood Emergency.||Radar-based rainfall estimates suggest that upwards of 14-16 of rain fell during this 5-day period in a narrow swath, with many more locations receiving 6-10 of rain. Most of this rain fell during the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th, which is when the most devastating impacts were felt. The highest totals occurred across an axis that stretches from northern Clay and southern Owsley counties, east through southern Breathitt and northern Leslie counties, into Perry, Knott and Letcher counties. The highest rainfall total report was from southern Knott County, where 14.00 fell between July 25th and July 29th. This site, a cooperative (COOP) observer at Carr Creek Lake, reported 6.71 from 7am July 28th to 7am July 29th, following a report of 6.50 at that site on the previous day. Another COOP site in Buckhorn reported 8.00 of rain for the 24-hour period ending 7am on July 28th. The rainfall total in Buckhorn from July 25th to July 29th was 11.76. These rainfall values occurring in such a short period of time are incredibly rare: there is less than a 1 in 1000 chance for this much rainfall over five days in a given year.||The incredible rainfall also led to significant rises and flooding on many rivers in eastern Kentucky including on the main stem of the Kentucky River; North, Middle and South forks of the Kentucky River; Red River and Licking River. At Whitesburg, the North Fork of the Kentucky River swelled well above major flood stage, reaching close to 21' before gauge failure (the previous flood of record was 14.7' in 1957). The North Fork of the Kentucky River at Jackson also reached major flood, setting a new record crest of 43.47' (the previous record was 43.1' set in 1939). The river flooding caused a second round of destruction for communities in the region, and caused flooding in downstream areas that did not receive as much rainfall.||*Note* Given the widespread nature and severity of this event - any dollar amount estimated by storm data will not do the event as a whole justice. Since eastern KY was a national declaration, FEMA will be doing a full cost assessment. Will use this data once available for total monetary amounts of damage.||Visit www.weather.gov/jkl/July2022Flooding for more information on the event, as well as pictures and videos of the flooding and damage.
episodes.172645: A push of monsoonal moisture resulted in sporadic flash flooding and isolated microbursts for the end of the month of July.
episodes.172678: The combination of near record moisture content (PWATs 1.8-2.0 inches), moderate to strong instability (SBCAPE  2000 J/KG), very slow steering flow and an upper-level disturbance resulted in a very conducive environment for the generation of thunderstorms producing very heavy rainfall activity across portions of south-central and southwestern Arizona, resulting in flash flooding. Activity first developed across the foothills and higher terrain of Eastern Maricopa and Gila Counties during the late morning-early afternoon hours. Another area of thunderstorms developed over northwestern Arizona during the mid-late afternoon hours and move southward towards La Paz County into the evening hours. One of the areas severely hit by flash flooding was Apache Junction, AZ. Weekes Wash, which runs through the town, went of out of its banks, causing widespread flooding impacts across the city. Flooding also took place from drainage that occurred off the Goldfield and Superstitions Mountains.
episodes.172688: Scattered slow moving thunderstorms developed over southeast Arizona during the morning and afternoon. Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in Pinal County, the Tucson Metro area and over the Contreras Fire burn scar.
episodes.172798: The heavy rain events of recent days in adjacent eastern Kentucky crossed into southwest Virginia on the 28th and produced significant flash flooding, especially around Pound VA.
episodes.172811: A warm front brought moist air into New Hampshire on the 25th and aided in thunderstorm development during the afternoon and early evening hours. A few storms were strong across southern New Hampshire.
episodes.172832: Multiple mesoscale convective vortices (MCVs) were seen across Arizona during the morning. Clearing skies allowed for daytime heating to add to the already unstable atmosphere.  As a result, there were multiple flash floods across the area.
episodes.172835: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Pittsburgh region with the passage of a shortwave trough. Sufficient moisture and instability led to brief, isolated downpours. Some thunderstorm segments had a storm motion which resulted in places receiving a quick inch or more in less than an hour. This resulted in isolated flash flooding in the Pittsburgh metro area.
episodes.172875: Deep monsoon moisture brought thunderstorms, heavy rain, and flash flooding across northern Arizona.
episodes.172912: A big push of monsoon moisture immediately followed the excessive heat event, and stormy conditions persisted into August. Several storms produced severe weather and flash flooding.
episodes.172913: The stormy period which began on the 24th continued to bring severe weather and flash flooding through the end of the month.
episodes.172915: The stormy period which began on the 24th continued to bring severe weather and flash flooding through the end of the month.
episodes.173004: A cluster of showers and thunderstorms, extending from St. Louis metro area to southeastern Missouri, moved eastward through the afternoon and early evening hours. With precipitable water values over 2 inches and warm cloud depths up to 14,000 feet thick, these storms produced very heavy rainfall, up to five inches, in a short period of time, between 2 pm and 7 pm on July 28th. Also, the soil in the area was quite saturated due to the catastrophic flash flooding two days prior. This caused another round of flash flooding in portions of St. Louis County, St. Louis city, Jefferson County in Missouri and St. Clair County in Illinois.

Approximately 50 people were unable to leave the Yankee Boy Basin area until the debris was cleared.

Flash flooding was reported on the north side of Tuba City washed away dirt roads and people had to be rescued from the water.
The hail was up to lime in size and occurred with wind gusts over 60 MPH that caused unspecified damage.  A total of 1.75 inches of rain occurred as well.

Pine tree approximately 10 inches in diameter was snapped off by the winds, and a cedar tree was broken into pieces.  There was also an unspecified amount of damage done to some buildings.  The winds occurred with hail up to limes in size.  A total of 1.75 inches of rain occurred.
Hail up to golf ball size occurred.  The hail also occurred with quite a bit of wind that blew branches down and caused considerable crop damage.
Tree limbs of an unspecified size were blown down.  These winds occurred with hail up to golf ball in size.
Six inches of water was observed running across County Road 44 at Highway 61.

Multiple reports of flash flooding were received across the eastern half of Letcher County. Flash flooding across portions of Letcher County persisted into areal flooding. In addition the river gauge at Whitesburg went from 2 feet around midnight on the 28th to a minor flood stage of 10 feet by 5:30 AM EST, then to a height of 22.03 feet by 10 AM EST. At this point the gauge was taken out by the flood waters before it crested. The river then dropped below flood stage once more later that afternoon around 5:45 PM EST.  ||Some additional flooding reports received for Letcher County between 7/28 and 7/29 include:||At 12:55 PM EST (7/28) - The Isom IGA/Subway is inundated by several feed of flood water. |At 1:46 PM EST - Pictures from the media show SKCTC Campus inundated by the North Fork of the Kentucky River. Water levels were half way up the first-story windows on at least one campus building.||Multiple other creeks and streams that fed into the North Fork of the Kentucky River also experienced extensive flooding.

Widespread damage occurred early Thursday morning across Minneapolis including: large tree trunks uprooted, tree trunks snapped, snapped power poles, a roof torn off a church, and window screens blown off the courthouse. After analysis of radar data, first-hand accounts and pictures, we conclude that straight-line winds of 95 mph produced this damage.
Report of part of large healthy tree blown down and onto the power lines which caused a power outage.

Flooding closed roadways near the intersection of Big Branch Rd and South Fork Rd, and a home was flooded. Minor flooding of businesses and the river gage house on Main Street. Flooding was also beginning in the Pound Bottom community, which was being monitored for potential evacuations.

Up to three to five inches of rainfall occurred in the area of Bethune and Stratton.  This area also received a couple inches of rainfall a couple days earlier.  Dispatch received three different reports of one to two feet of water over county roads in this area.  In two of these reports the water extended for 10 to 20 feet over the road.  No damage was reported.

Flash flooding across Breathitt County then led to areal flooding, and record flooding of the North Fork Kentucky River at Jackson. Before the flooding, the North Fork was about 10 feet. Within a few hours, at 5 AM EST on July 28, it reached minor flood stage of 29 feet. It then went on to crest at a record 43.47 feet at 1:30 AM EST July 29th. It fell below flood stage later that day around noon EST. ||Some other flood reports that were received across the county during this time include: ||08:53 AM EST - Kiwanis Park in Jackson was inundated by the North Fork Kentucky River.|09:16 AM EST - Homes in the Lost Creek Community, as well as the Riverside School campus, are inundated by flood waters from Troublesome and Lost Creeks. |1:00 PM EST - A picture shows Canoe Road inundated by the Middle Fork of the Kentucky River in the Canoe community. |2:00 PM EST - KY-52 is also inundated.  |9:25 AM EST - Jackson Save-A-Lot and Tractor Supply Co. were inundated by the North Fork Kentucky River. |9:47 AM EST - Pictures show the North Fork Kentucky River inundating Slones Trailer Park up to the windows of a car. ||Multiple other creeks and streams that fed into the North Fork Kentucky River also experienced extensive flooding.
No damage was reported but confidence was high that severe level wind gusts occurred.

Cranes Nest River near the town of Clintwood rose above its 13 foot bankfull level during the morning hours of July 28th. The river crested at 17.2 feet that evening and then returned to its banks a few hours later. This resulted in sections of Route 649 observing high water, along with several camps along the river.
US-23 Business Route south of Pound was flooded in several places. Riverside Drive in the Pound Bottom community was flooded near the hairpin turn.

Several small residential bridges were washed out north of Clintwood. Brush Creek rose out of its banks and spilled onto Brush Creek Road. Bear Pen Creek also rose out of its banks, flooding to adjacent roadway and the nearby park.
Dickenson Highway was flooded in several spots between Clintwood and Clinchco, closing the road for a brief period of time.

Creek flooding along South Mountain Road washed away the asphalt from the road next to Lone Pine Chapel Church, and washed out some of the ground beneath some foundation pillars of a veterinary hospital next door.
Rock Switch Rd near Guest River Rd was impassable due to flood waters of the Guest River.
Route 23 was closed between Pound and Wise because of flooding. Shelter was being opened for those who had been evacuated.

Runoff from heavy rains eventually found their way to to the Right Fork of Beaver Creek in southwest Floyd County, and Beaver Creek near Martin, leading to multiple reports of flooding in communities near the water. Some reports included:||At 8:30 AM EST - Pictures show the Marathon Gas Station along KY-7 (Main Street) in Wayland inundated by flood waters. Fuel pumps were completely submerged. |At 3:14 PM EST - Video footage showed a water rescue by the bridge on KY-7 near Maddy's Pizza in Hueysville.|At 4:00 PM EST - A picture on social media showed water up to the windows on trailer homes in Hueysville.|At 4:19 PM EST - The Garret community was reported to be inundated by several feet of flood waters from the Right Fork Beaver Creek.|At 6:28 PM EST - The Martin Fire Department reported flood waters over Brawley Street in Martin.

The Red River was running high through Wolfe County. At 09:00 AM EST there was a report that the Red River was flooding across KY-205 at Lee City. At 11:38 AM EST a second report was made of several inches of standing water from the Red River in the Wolfe County Animal Shelter.
Swift water rescues occurred, including along Business Route 23 at Kanawha Rd.

A tornado touched down in Wyoming County at approximately 10:40AM EDT in the town of Java just southwest of the intersection of NY Route 78 and Chaffee Rd. The tornado then moved along an east-northeast path near NY Route 78 for approximately 10 miles before dissipating in the western portion of the Town of Gainesville just west of NY Route 19 at about 10:55 AM EDT. The tornado was on the ground for approximately 15 minutes.||The tornado reached a maximum intensity of EF-2, with winds of 115 mph. The maximum path width was about 500 yards. The majority of the EF-2 rated damage was along the first two miles of the tornado path. This was also the portion of the track with the most consistent and continuous damage. In this portion of the track, the tornado did significant damage to a barn. The older portion of the barn saw its concrete block foundation toppled and the structure itself moved about 25 feet. The newer portion of the barn was entirely destroyed. Multiple hard and softwood trees were uprooted or saw their trunks sheared off as the tornado tracked along NY Route 78 until it got to|about Pleasant Valley Road. ||Damage became all EF-1 or lower rated to the east of Pleasant Valley Road through Hermitage. This included a few uprooted softwood trees and some minor wall damage to a structure on Shaw Road. ||As the tornado crossed from the Town of Wethersfield and into the western portion of the Town of Gainesville, damage became much less continuous and likely indicative of a discontinuous path of the tornado. All damage on this eastern extend of the path was minor tree damage and rated EF-0 before damage ceased about one mile west|of NY Route 19.
Water rescue needed along the Guest River near Coeburn.

Between 1 and 3 inches of rain fell within 1-2 hours across Apache Junction and the adjacent higher terrain north and east of the city, towards the Goldfield and Superstitions mountains. Water from those mountains drained down towards the area washes, including Weekes Wash, which runs through the city. Numerous roads were flooded and damaged along with multiple water rescues taking place of residents in homes that either were surrounded with water or had water inside them. One of the more dramatic water rescues occurred when a woman had to be rescued from her vehicle that was swept away by the flood waters of Weekes Wash and traveled half a mile downstream before encountering a box culvert. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 in 90 minutes over the Contreras Fire burn scar caused a 1-2 ft debris flow across State Highway 386 to Kitt Peak.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down several trees and wires.

A video posted on social media showed strong flow moving along the Bloody Tanks Wash, resulting a street crossing the wash near Mackey Camp to be completely impassable. No damages or injuries were reported.

Thunderstorms produced heavy precipitation over the Tank Hollow Fire burn scar, with 1-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor estimates of 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rain. Associated with this, the Dispatch Center in the city of Price reported running water and debris along U.S. Highway 6 from mileposts 197 to 198. It was further reported that dirt and mud was a foot deep, with tree trunks and logs 8 to 10 inches in diameter included in the debris.
Social media video showed Bloody Tanks Wash in major elevated stage as it was flowing down the city of Miami. No damages or injuries were reported.
The Arizona Department of Transportation reported SR 88 was closed due to flooding between milepost 201 and 205. No damages or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree branch onto the roof of a house. The roof sustained minor damage.

Up to five inches fell in a three hour period causing flash flooding across the northern half of the city of St. Louis. Numerous roads were flooded including Washington Avenue near the intersection with Walton Avenue, south bound Skinker near Forest Park, Lindell Boulevard near Vandeventer Avenue, South Vandeventer Avenue just south of I-64 and Kingshighway Boulevard between Natural Bridge Avenue and St. Louis Avenue. Flash flooding in the 4700 block of Washington Avenue flooded a local daycare. The fire department had to rescue 15 children and 3 adults from the facility. No injuries were reported. Also, several dozen motorists had to be rescued from their flooded vehicles. Five city schools were damaged due to flooding. The flooding affected schools from north St. Louis to south. Soldan High School had at least 2 feet of water in the cafeteria on the basement floor. At least 4 businesses sustained water damage from the flooding in the Central West End. Both directions of Interstate 64 at Hampton Avenue and eastbound Interstate 70 at Union Boulevard were closed for part of the afternoon due to flooding.

Water Users Recreation Site just downstream of Saguaro Lake was closed due to flash flooding and debris deposited into the Lower Salt River, making the water unsafe for public use. No injuries were reported.
Heavy rain of 2-3 in 90 minutes in Aravaipa Canyon caused a debris flow and flash flood along the creek through the wilderness area.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a three hour period causing flash flooding across the eastern portions of St. Louis County, including University City, Glendale, Brentwood and Maplewood areas. Numerous roads were flooded including McKnight Road where Deer Creek flows under it, Olive Blvd. and Skinker Blvd. intersection, and Waldron Avenue north of Olive Blvd.
Winds caused minor damage to the Southern Bancorp building in Bismarck.
Street flooding was reported along Jefferson Highway in Baton Rouge.

Delayed report...The press box was blown off of the bleachers at the Bismarck High School Football Field. Additional damage was done to a gas station awning off of Hwy. 84 and Hwy. 7. The time was estimated by radar.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 2 hours over the Santa Catalina Mountains caused flash flooding in San Manuel and nearby areas with several dirt roads washed out.

Up to three inches fell in a 4 hour period causing flash flooding. Numerous roads were flooded across the northern half of St. Clair County, including Main Street at West Highway 50 in O'Fallon, Illinois Route 15 at Belleville West Parkway, and northbound I-55/I-70 in East St. Louis. Several families had to be rescued from their homes due to the flash flooding, including one on State Street and one on Terrace Drive in East St. Louis. No injuries were reported.
North Lake Rd along Bartlett Lake was closed due to flooding and debris making the road impassable to vehicular traffic. No injuries were reported.

Up to three inches of rain fell in about an hour and a half causing flash flooding. Several roads in far northern portions of Jefferson County were briefly flooded. One vehicle became stuck in flood waters after being driven into the flooded section of roadway, about 3 miles southeast of Murphy. No injuries were reported.

An EF-0 tornado touched down about 2 miles south-southwest of Dennis Hill State Park along Smith Road and traveled northeastward for about 5 miles before ending about 2 miles southwest of Colebrook along Pinney Street. Damage was sporadic and consisted mostly of downed hardwood trees and broken tree branches. A couple of barns along Pinney Street lost some siding and one of the barns had a door torn off. There were many eye witnesses which provided both video and pictures of the tornado.
